newsitem.title: FINLAND: NEW FINNISH COMPANIES ACT ALLOWS SHARE BUY-BACKS.
newsitem.headline: NEW FINNISH COMPANIES ACT ALLOWS SHARE BUY-BACKS.

text.p: Finland's new limited companies act will allow joint stock companies to buy back and sell their own shares, overturning an old rule against the practice, the justice ministry said on Friday.

"For public companies the maximum amount of (own) shares that can be bought and held in a company's portfolio is five percent of the voting shares," justice ministry official Jyrki Jauhiainen told a briefing.
This would amount to no more than five percent of total outstanding shares in terms of nominal value or votes, the ministry said in a statement.
The limit will not apply to shares aquired through mergers, and if shares are cancelled, then a company can buy more, Jauhiainen said.
"The opportunity to buy back and sell their own shares will increase the financing means available to companies," the ministry said in a statement.
The legislation will take effect on September 1.
Companies can only buy their own shares with distributable earnings, and they must announce at least one week in advance their plans to buy their own shares on the open market, the ministry said.
Unless they are calcelled, redeemed shares must be sold three years after they were purchased, and sales of a company's own shares will be subject to rules similar to those regulating share issues.
Industry -- particularly forest industry firms which have often seen their shares undervalued -- have long been calling for the possibility to purhcase their own shares.

The corporations act reform also includes a clutch of new rules on share capital, group structure, reporting obligations, mergers and minority buyouts, as well as a new distinction between public and private companies.
It also introduces new financial instruments such as non-voting preferred shares and capital notes.

Once the law is in place, public companies' names will end with the abbreviation Oyj (Abp in Swedish) for "julkinen osakeyhtio" or "publikt aktiebolag," instead of just Oy or Ab which will be carried by private limited companies.
Under the new rules, public companies must register a share capital of at least 500,000 markka and the minimum required for private companies will be raised to 50,000 markka from 15,000.
